en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on the Analysis of Formless Phenomena: 16.
The Question on the Difficulty of Analyzing Formless Phenomena
The king said:
“Venerable Nāgasena, was it indeed difficult for the Blessed One to perform?
The Elder replied:
“It was difficult, Great King, that was done by the Blessed One.
“But what, venerable Nāgasena, was difficult that was done by the Blessed One?
“Difficult, Great King, was that done by the Blessed One: that these formless mental states—the mind and its concomitants—[should be made] to have a single object.”
“The defining of those [factors] as they occur has been declared: ‘This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.
“Give me a simile,” [the king said].
“It is just as if, great king, some man were to plunge into the great ocean by boat and, with the hollow of his hand, take up water.”
“Having taken it up and tasted it with his tongue, O Great King, would that man be able to know:
‘This is the water of the Ganges, this is the water of the Yamunā, this is the water of the Aciravatī, this is the water of the Sarabhū, this is the water of the Mahī’?
“It would be difficult, venerable sir, to know,” he replied.
“Even more difficult than this, Great King, was performed by the Blessed One:
the defining of these formless mental states and mental factors as they occur upon a single object, declaring:
‘This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.’”
“Very well, venerable sir,” the king replied in approval.
This was the sixteenth question on the difficulty of defining formless phenomena.
This was the seventh chapter on the definition of formless phenomena.
In this chapter, there are sixteen questions.
